identity.title: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Memorize: The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regularization in Training

problem.claim: Understand how diffusion-model training dynamics govern the transition between generalization and memorization.

gap.claim: The mechanisms preventing memorization while enabling generalization remain insufficiently understood.

contributions.claim: Identify distinct generation and memorization timescales, with memorization delayed proportionally to training-set size while generation onset stays constant.
Characterize the resulting training-time window as implicit dynamical regularization that can avoid memorization in highly overparameterized settings.
Support the findings with experiments on standard U-Nets and realistic and synthetic datasets, alongside a high-dimensional random-features analysis.

stated_novelty.claim: The work presents implicit dynamical regularization through distinct generation and memorization timescales as an explanation for diffusion models’ resistance to memorization.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that high-quality generation begins at an early time τ_gen, whereas memorization emerges only after a later time τ_mem.
The authors report that τ_mem grows linearly with training-set size n while τ_gen remains constant, producing a widening effective-generalization window.
The authors report that overfitting disappears at infinite training times only when n exceeds a model-dependent threshold.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper frames the unresolved question of why diffusion models generalize without memorizing training data.
It examines whether training dynamics control the transition from generalization to memorization.
It identifies early generation and later memorization timescales, with only the latter scaling linearly with dataset size.
The scaling creates a dataset-size-dependent training window and is interpreted as implicit dynamical regularization, supported by experiments and tractable theory.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates generation onset from memorization onset and explicitly relates their scaling behavior to training-set size.

lessons.interpretation: Separating when desired behavior appears from when failure behavior emerges can make a mechanistic claim more precise.
lessons.application: Report separate onset metrics and their scaling with dataset size when studying training-time tradeoffs.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the relevant behaviors lack identifiable onset times or cannot be measured consistently.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the numerical slopes, definitions, or measurement procedures for τ_gen and τ_mem.
The model-dependent threshold in S7 is not quantified, and the scope across architectures or datasets beyond those tested is unclear.
The abstract does not provide detailed experimental results or theoretical assumptions needed to assess the strength of the reported claims.
